opus-5.5.text:
I think it's useful to separate the question into a few layers, because people often lump everything together under "compute constraints" when there are really distinct bottlenecks that bind at different scales and on different timelines.

On the technical side, the first thing to look at is chip production. Most frontier AI chips run through a very concentrated supply chain: advanced logic fabrication at a handful of fabs, advanced packaging capacity, and high-bandwidth memory from a small number of suppliers. Over the last few years, packaging and HBM have arguably been tighter bottlenecks than the leading-edge wafers themselves. These are things you can expand, but fabs and packaging lines take years to build and billions of dollars to equip, so there's real lag between demand signals and supply response.

The second major technical constraint is power. If you extrapolate the growth in training runs, which has been something like four to five times more compute per year for frontier models, you quickly get to individual training runs needing gigawatts of power. That's the scale of a large power plant. You can get there through some combination of building new generation, locating near existing underused capacity, and distributing training across multiple data centers in different regions. But each of those has costs. Distributed training adds communication overhead, and new generation runs into grid interconnection queues that in the US can stretch for years.

Then there are more fundamental limits further out, like data movement and latency within a training run. As you scale up, you need to keep huge numbers of chips synchronized, and at some point the time it takes to pass information around becomes a binding constraint on how large and how fast a single run can be. My sense is those limits are real but probably not binding this decade. You can push quite far before you hit them.

On the regulatory side, I'd say the most important constraints today aren't AI-specific regulations at all. They're things like permitting for power plants and transmission lines, environmental review, zoning for data centers, and grid interconnection rules. Those were designed for a very different world, and they can add years to projects. Export controls are the other big one, and they're explicitly about compute: restricting where advanced chips and chipmaking equipment can go shapes which actors can scale and how fast.

When we've tried to estimate this, the picture I come away with is that none of these individually looks like a hard wall in the near term. It seems feasible, if companies keep investing, to sustain current growth rates for training compute through roughly the end of the decade. But power and chip manufacturing capacity look like the most likely places where things get tight first. And the regulatory environment matters a lot for whether those bottlenecks get resolved in two years or seven.

So I'd frame it as: the physics and engineering permit a lot more scaling, the economics will determine whether people are willing to pay for it, and policy, especially energy policy, determines how much friction there is along the way.

r001.rationale: The response describes years-long fab and packaging expansion delays, but does not identify demand signals propagating through multiple supply-chain companies as the constraint.

r002.rationale: It identifies concentrated dependence on advanced logic fabrication, advanced packaging, and high-bandwidth memory, and describes packaging and memory as bottlenecks to expanding supply.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that there are really a few distinct layers of constraint, and they operate on quite different timescales.

The first and most immediate is the hardware supply chain itself. The entire frontier of AI compute runs through a remarkably narrow pipeline: TSMC for the leading-edge nodes, ASML for the EUV lithography tools, and then a small number of memory suppliers for high-bandwidth memory, which has actually become one of the tightest bottlenecks. And then there's advanced packaging, CoWoS and similar, which has repeatedly been the thing that actually limited how many accelerators got shipped in a given quarter. So even if demand and capital are there, you can't just conjure up another few million H100-class chips. Fabs take years to build and the expertise is concentrated in a handful of firms.

The second layer is energy and physical infrastructure. If you extrapolate the roughly 4x per year growth in training compute that we've seen over the last decade or so, you quite quickly get to training runs that would require gigawatts of power. That's a meaningful fraction of a large country's grid. Securing that kind of power, getting the interconnects approved, building the cooling and the datacenter shells, these things run into permitting processes and utility planning cycles that are measured in years, not months. I think this is where a lot of the real friction will emerge over the next five years, more than from chips per se.

Then there's the regulatory layer, which so far has mostly been expressed through export controls rather than domestic limits. The US controls on advanced chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment to China are the clearest example. Those don't constrain global compute so much as redistribute who gets access to it. Domestically, we've seen things like reporting thresholds tied to training compute, the 10^26 FLOP figure for instance, but those are mostly transparency measures rather than hard caps. Whether that evolves into something more binding is an open question, and I think it partly depends on whether the capability trends continue to look as dramatic as they have.

And finally there's the economic constraint, which people sometimes underrate. Scaling compute at the current rate means training costs growing into the tens of billions, then hundreds of billions of dollars. That's only sustainable if the revenue follows. So far it largely has, but at some point the question of whether the returns justify the next order of magnitude becomes the binding one, well before you hit hard physical limits.

So my overall view is that none of these are walls in the near term. We can probably sustain something like the current growth rate for several more years. But the constraints compound, and by the early 2030s I'd expect energy and capital to be the dominant factors, with regulation potentially layered on top depending on how governments respond to what these systems can do.

r001.rationale: The response says fabs take years to build and names a concentrated supply chain, but does not identify the time required for demand signals to propagate among its companies.

r002.rationale: It identifies concentrated expertise in a handful of firms, alongside specialized inputs such as leading-edge lithography, high-bandwidth memory, and advanced packaging, as constraints on expanding chip supply.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between constraints on producing more compute and constraints on who can access it.

On the production side, there’s a whole supply chain that has to expand. You need advanced chips, the equipment and facilities to manufacture them, memory, networking, and then data centers with sufficient power and cooling. Increasing investment helps, but these things have different lead times. You can order more chips much faster than you can build a new fabrication plant or expand electricity infrastructure.

There’s also a technical question about how effectively you can use all that hardware. Doubling the number of chips doesn’t necessarily halve the time it takes to train a model. You have to communicate between chips, distribute the work efficiently, and handle failures. Those challenges become more significant as clusters grow. Algorithmic improvements can push in the other direction, allowing you to achieve a given capability with less compute.

On the regulatory side, export controls can restrict access to advanced chips and the equipment used to make them. Permitting and electricity regulation can also affect how quickly new data centers come online. So regulation can constrain compute without taking the form of a direct limit on AI training.

The important distinction is that restricting access in one country or for one organization isn’t necessarily the same as reducing the total amount of compute available globally. It might instead change where that compute is deployed. So when we talk about a constraint, we should ask: a constraint on whose access, over what time horizon, and on physical hardware or on the useful computation you can get out of it?

r001.rationale: The response mentions supply-chain expansion and differing lead times, but does not identify demand signals propagating through multiple semiconductor companies as the constraint.

r002.rationale: It identifies advanced chips and the equipment and facilities needed to manufacture them as necessary supply-chain inputs, and says their differing lead times constrain how quickly compute can expand.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between constraints on building more compute and constraints on bringing that compute together into a single training run.

On the first, you have the supply of advanced chips, the capacity to manufacture them, and then power and data centers. You can invest more money, but that doesn’t immediately give you a new semiconductor fab or a connection to the electricity grid. There are lead times, and permitting can make those substantially longer. So even if demand is very strong, the supply response takes time.

Then there’s the technical question of how efficiently you can use all those chips. You don’t get twice the useful computation simply by buying twice as many GPUs. They need to communicate, and as you scale up, communication and synchronization can become bottlenecks. That’s particularly challenging if you want to spread training across geographically separated data centers. The network between them is much slower than the connections within a cluster.

On the regulatory side, export controls affect who can obtain advanced chips and the equipment needed to manufacture them. Other rules could constrain the construction of data centers or impose requirements on very large training runs. Those are different interventions: restricting access to hardware is different from requiring a developer to evaluate a model before deploying it.

So I wouldn’t describe compute as having one fixed ceiling. There are several constraints, operating over different timescales. Some can be relaxed through investment or engineering; others depend on policy. And improvements in algorithms mean that even a constraint on physical compute doesn’t translate directly into a fixed limit on AI capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response mentions manufacturing lead times, but does not identify demand signals propagating through multiple semiconductor supply-chain companies as a constraint.

r002.rationale: The response names chips, manufacturing capacity, power, and data centers, but does not identify highly specialized talent or inputs as a supply-chain bottleneck.
